extracted.intended_audience: improvisers and improvisation teachers (performers, students, comedy practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical standards and teaching guidance for performing, directing, and developing improvised theatre and comedy (short- and long-form). Covers core principles (listening, yes-and, making choices), anti-patterns, rehearsal/process guidance, and how to push the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to what the person wants and give it to them
rubrics_metrics.description: You listen to what the person wants and then you give it to them. (Charna Halpern: “You listen to what the person wants and then you give it to them.”)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat offers as information about desire/need and supply that information. Example: if a partner offers “I’ll pay for dinner” and implies ‘no sex tonight,’ react to the underlying information. Anti-pattern: ignoring partner offers or trying to redirect rather than respond to their wants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes‑and / give information (do not only ask questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic idea is you have to give information — that’s the yes-and principle. Asking questions is fine only if the question itself adds useful information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good questions add scene information (e.g., “How are we going to find food now that we’re stranded?”). Bad patterns: asking neutral questions like “What are we doing?” that provide nothing, or being taught to mechanically 'say yes' to offers that are damaging (e.g., an offer to 'kill yourself').

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement is between actors, not characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreement that makes scenes work is an agreement between the actors (their collaboration), not between the fictional characters they play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing relieves actors and focuses responsibility on mutual support. Use it to justify safe refusals of offers that would harm the actor or scene while still maintaining ensemble agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen and react / be present
rubrics_metrics.description: Listening and genuine reacting are essential — improvisation works when you hear and react, not when you are 'already thinking of your next line.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence is also core to good acting. Train to stay in the moment and respond to subtext. Anti-patterns: performers who trivialize offers, fail to react emotionally, or seem preoccupied with their next joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make choices that surprise from your point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: An improviser must be invited to make choices; choices should surprise but be truthful to the character's point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bland sense-making; make surprising, specific choices that arise from your perspective. This keeps scenes interesting and prevents boredom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support your partner and make them look good
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers are trained to make their partner look good; ensemble caretaking is fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize offers that help your partner succeed. 'Look after your partner' and 'make each other look good' are repeated norms. At the same time, some schools encourage individuals to 'support themselves' — balance ensemble care with individual clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't try to be funny; embrace failure and be relaxed
rubrics_metrics.description: Trying to be funny often gets in the way. Failure (failing good-naturedly) is part of the form — be relaxed and let fun emerge from risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences enjoy seeing performers in genuine risk, provided actors appear okay. Anti-pattern: anxious trying-too-hard performances that make audiences uncomfortable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid templates, clichés and recycled 'safe' choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced improvisers should push beyond recycled templates (generic restaurants, default first-dates, stock characters) rather than settling for safe, familiar options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Templates arise from cultural training and media. To innovate, deliberately use unfamiliar settings, mistakes (verbal slips), or specific detail rather than generic placeholders. Anti-pattern: reliance on the same stock scenes and props leading to monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the audience in mind; avoid indulgence and 'bag of tricks'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not forget the audience — performers who become indulgent, pull out the same tricks, or 'phone it in' produce mediocre shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotate collaborators, avoid over-rehearsed tricks, and keep danger and surprise so the audience is engaged. Anti-patterns: repeating gags, playing only with the same people, planning set pieces every show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and use form (short form, long form, Harold, Theatresports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that short-form games, long-form plays, the Harold, and Theatresports each have different dynamics; many short-form games appear inside long-form structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't create artificial rifts between schools — use elements (e.g., subtitles, narrative devices) from short form inside the Harold. Assess which format fits your goals and allow cross-pollination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break adult/rational patterns to find play (trick your adult brain)
rubrics_metrics.description: To escape ruts, trick the adult/rational part of your brain using devices like starting a scene with a sound, leading with an odd body part, starting in the middle, or deciding a thought and changing it at the last moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These techniques force spontaneity and stimulate the childlike playfulness that improvisation needs. Use exercises to disrupt habitual patterns rather than overthinking solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be fearless: love failure and constantly quest for the unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of embarrassment, rejection, or being liked holds improvisers back; you must love failure and be willing to try things you haven't done before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek risky, unfamiliar offers (e.g., odd settings, strange characters). If you avoid discomfort you will stagnate; taking risks leads to growth and innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and draw widely from literature/art/world events to enrich material
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and absorb from books, theatre, psychology, literature and other arts to give depth to improvisation beyond surface comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating genre-based work research the genre (e.g., horror, Sondheim) so the improvisation can play with conventions intelligently. Anti-pattern: limiting improvisation input to current TV/sketch culture only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rehearsal and collaborative diagnostic process to innovate
rubrics_metrics.description: When developing new shows, admit where you are stuck, discuss goals as a group, research the genre, and then explore in rehearsal until you reach discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process is iterative: say where you are, research, try, fail, play, and refine until 'ah‑ha' moments occur. Keep intervention minimal unless invited; support as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when not to enter; being asked to play is a mark of a good improviser
rubrics_metrics.description: Not entering a scene can be as important as entering. A sign of a good improviser is that peers want to play with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you're frequently not asked to play, solicit feedback from peers about what to improve. Practice skills (endowments, characters) and be mindful of timing and scene contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take from many schools; don't protect a single dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should learn from all available teachings and not rigidly defend a single guru or school of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine useful elements from Del Close, Keith Johnstone, Spolin, Theatresports, Annoyance, etc., to develop a well-rounded approach. Avoid tribalism that prevents adopting helpful techniques.
